analysis.investment_thesis: Aarti Industries has experienced a catastrophic earnings collapse — net profit fell from INR 1,186 Cr in FY22 to just INR 331 Cr in FY25 (-72%), while ROE has cratered to 6% on a bloated capital base. A 43x P/E on deteriorating fundamentals violates every principle of growth investing.
key_strengths: OCF positive in all 5 years (INR 873–1,319 Cr range), showing the underlying chemical operations do generate cash
Specialty chemicals China+1 thesis offers a structural tailwind for Indian benzene-chain manufacturers with long-term export potential
Revenue base grew from INR 3,006 Cr (FY16) to INR 7,271 Cr (FY25), indicating the business has genuine scale
key_risks: Net profit has collapsed 72% from peak: INR 1,186 Cr (FY22) → INR 545 Cr (FY23) → INR 416 Cr (FY24) → INR 331 Cr (FY25) — this is the opposite of the growth trajectory Fisher demands
ROE of 6.03% and ROCE of 6.32% are deeply sub-par; the company earns less than its cost of capital on an ever-growing asset base of INR 11,702 Cr
Capex of INR 1,386 Cr in FY25 against OCF of INR 1,242 Cr yields persistent negative FCF — heavy capital deployment is not translating into earnings growth
red_flags: 9-year net profit CAGR of just 2.4% — revenues grew 10.3% but earnings barely moved, indicating severe margin deterioration and capital misallocation
EBITDA contracting trend: peaked at INR 1,687 Cr in FY22, falling to INR 986 Cr in FY25 despite higher revenues
Finance cost has nearly tripled from INR 86 Cr (FY21) to INR 275 Cr (FY25) while profits collapsed — debt is growing, returns are shrinking
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Aarti Industries is a classic example of a business I would have found attractive in 2021 — strong specialty chemical franchise, India export story, rising margins — but the intervening years have revealed structural problems. Margins have been destroyed by a combination of commodity chemical pricing pressure, aggressive capacity expansion without demand support, and rising finance costs. The EBITDA contracting trend with simultaneously negative FCF tells me this capex cycle has been badly timed and executed.

From a Fisher perspective, the critical question is whether management has the capability to restore returns. With ROE at 6%, they are destroying shareholder value on net. At a P/E of 43x, the market is still pricing in an optimistic recovery that the data does not support. I see no innovation moat that differentiates this company — benzene-chain chemistry is largely commoditized — and the 9-year earnings CAGR of 2.4% confirms this is a cyclical, not a growth, business. I avoid at this valuation.
